row.basis: God's Spirit and words placed in a mouth, never departing
row.note: The commentary takes 87:6 as God's promise to make the recipient recite and retain the given word. Isaiah's covenant places God's Spirit and words in a recipient's mouth and promises that they will not leave that mouth or its descendants, extending secure recitation into a line of transmission.

row.basis: a song written, taught, and put in Israel's mouth
row.note: The commentary's instructor first gives the recitation and the recipient then carries it. God tells Moses to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths; the verse combines written preservation, teaching, and voiced reception.

row.basis: the covenant song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The promised “you will not forget” is a result of divine action in the commentary. Deuteronomy makes the song a witness precisely because it will not be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a communal analogue to retained recitation.

row.basis: the Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: The commentary insists that unforgetting is granted rather than commanded. Jesus promises that the Paraclete will teach the disciples and bring all his sayings to their remembrance, a direct Christian promise of divinely caused recall.

row.basis: YHWH with Moses' mouth, teaching what to speak
row.note: The direct divine “we” and enabled human speech are central to the commentary. At Moses' reluctance, YHWH promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, making speech possible without making Moses its independent source.

row.basis: YHWH puts words into a prophet's mouth
row.note: The commentary pictures the word moving from its source into the recipient's tongue. In Jeremiah's call, YHWH touches the prophet's mouth and says that the divine words have been put there, a particularly close prophetic counterpart.

row.basis: taught tongue and repeatedly awakened ear
row.note: The commentary's causative reading has the recipient hear the teacher before speaking for others. Isaiah's servant receives a taught tongue and an ear awakened morning by morning to hear as a learner, joining receptive hearing to fitting speech.

row.basis: the Holy Spirit teaches what must be said
row.note: The commentary treats 87:6 as a future assurance that God enables the addressee's utterance. Jesus tells disciples that the Holy Spirit will teach them, at the needed moment, what they ought to say; the setting is different, but the divine provision of speech is equally explicit.

row.basis: word in mouth and heart for enactment
row.note: The commentary describes the given word as held within the recipient and then given outwardly. Deuteronomy says the command is very near, in mouth and heart, in order to do it; it joins inner retention, oral expression, and lived obedience.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's B001/B002 labels develop ق ر ء as recitation that carries joined words to hearers. Moses reads the covenant book aloud to Israel in this verse; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ) is the clear cognate and its covenant setting shows reading as received, binding speech.

row.basis: a scroll eaten before the prophet speaks
row.note: The commentary's womb-and-heart image has revelation taken inside before it is released as public speech. Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then go speak to Israel, making ingestion the concrete bridge between receiving written words and proclaiming them.

row.basis: words received from God spoken to Israel
row.note: After the scroll scene, Ezekiel is sent to Israel with God's own words. This supplies the outward half of the commentary's sequence: a word retained in the prophet becomes warning addressed to others.

row.basis: the little scroll eaten, sweet in mouth and bitter within
row.note: The commentary compares a word held in the body to a pregnancy before its outward delivery. Revelation recasts Ezekiel's act: John takes and eats a scroll, experiencing it in mouth and stomach, an embodied reception of prophecy rather than mere reading.

row.basis: prophecy required after eating the scroll
row.note: The commentary moves from retained recitation to the task of reminding others. After the scroll is eaten, John is told that he must prophesy again about peoples and kings; this supplies the public-release side of the same received-word image.

row.basis: Torah placed within and written on hearts
row.note: The commentary says that the word is gathered and held in the recipient rather than merely external to him. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise has God put Torah within the people and write it on their hearts, a scriptural inner-inscription analogue.

row.basis: the word dwelling richly, teaching, admonishing, and singing
row.note: The commentary links unforgotten recitation to later reminder, worship, and a life shaped by the word. Colossians asks that Christ's word dwell richly in the community so that it teaches and admonishes through sung praise, joining inward residence to communal utterance.

row.basis: the good deposit guarded through the indwelling Spirit
row.note: The commentary calls the received word an entrusted deposit whose retention depends on the giver. Timothy is told to guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers, a Christian account of preserved teaching with divine, not merely human, custody.

row.basis: Arabic ن س ي B001/B002/B003 and Hebrew נשה (nāšâ)
row.note: The commentary's ن س ي material makes forgetting both failure to retain an entrusted word and, through the womb image, a falling-away from what was held. Deuteronomy says Israel is unmindful of the Rock that begot it and forgets the God who gave it birth; Hebrew נשה (nāšâ) is cognate with Arabic ن س ي, and the verse uniquely joins forgetting to birthing.

row.basis: a nursing mother who might forget, but God does not
row.note: The commentary contrasts human forgetfulness with the God who does not forget, while using maternal containment as a secondary image. Isaiah invokes a nursing mother and her child only to insist that even if she forgets, God will not forget Zion, binding maternal care and unfailing divine memory.

row.basis: do not forget what was received; make it known to children
row.note: The commentary's recipient is preserved from forgetting so that he can later remind others. Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget what it has witnessed and immediately turns that memory into teaching children and grandchildren, giving a covenantal counterpart to retention becoming reminder.

row.basis: withered grass and the word that stands forever
row.note: The commentary places the promise that the recited word will not fall away beside pasture turned into dark refuse. Isaiah's one verse contrasts grass and flower fading with God's word standing forever, making the vegetation-to-enduring-word relationship unusually close.

row.basis: the enduring word identified as announced good news
row.note: The commentary joins an unfailing word to its passage from the recipient to other hearers. Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it as the good news announced to the audience, coupling permanence with oral proclamation.

row.basis: a burned scroll recreated and expanded by dictation
row.note: The commentary grounds preservation in the divine source rather than the recipient's unaided memory. After Jehoiakim burns the first scroll, Jeremiah dictates its former words to another scroll and additional words are added; the scene tests the durability of revealed wording against material loss.

row.basis: God's word goes from the divine mouth and accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary presents the recited speech as originating with God and reaching its assigned result. Isaiah's word goes out from God's mouth, does not return empty, and accomplishes the sender's purpose, a source-to-effect account of effective revelation.

row.basis: the book kept in the mouth, meditated on, and enacted
row.note: The commentary rejects a reading that remains only on the tongue and ends with recitation joined to worshipful practice. Joshua is told that the book of Torah must not depart from his mouth, but be meditated on day and night so that he does what is written; it makes durable recitation a form of life.

row.basis: prophets speaking from God while carried by the Spirit
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the human reader from the God who supplies the word. Second Peter says prophetic speech did not arise by human will but that people spoke from God while borne by the Holy Spirit, expressing a comparable account of sourced prophetic utterance.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary treats recitation as joined words whose meaning is also opened for hearers. Nehemiah's assembly reads from the Torah and gives its sense so the people understand the reading; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ), cognate with the commentary's ق ر ء, appears in a communal reading-and-explanation setting.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's recitation is held so that it governs the recipient's way of life. The king must keep a Torah scroll with him and read it all his days in order to learn reverence and keep its words; the Hebrew cognate קרא makes daily reading an antidote to abandonment.

row.basis: God's word stored in the heart
row.note: The commentary says the word is gathered within so it will not be lost. The psalmist stores God's saying in the heart in order not to sin, a devotional response that makes inner retention ethically consequential.

row.basis: one reader, hearers, and keepers of prophecy
row.note: The commentary traces a word from its divine source through a reader to those reminded by it. Revelation blesses the one who reads its prophecy aloud and those who hear and keep it, a liturgical community shaped by public recitation and retention.

row.basis: Christ's letter written by the Spirit on human hearts
row.note: The commentary's pages are not opposed to interior retention: words are gathered in the recipient before they are uttered. Paul calls the Corinthian community Christ's letter, written by the living God's Spirit on hearts rather than stone, a Christian transformation of scroll imagery into inward inscription.

row.basis: Deuteronomy's mouth-and-heart word read as proclaimed faith
row.note: The commentary brings a word into the mouth and heart before it goes out to others. Paul quotes the mouth-and-heart formulation of Deuteronomy and explicitly identifies it as the word of faith that he proclaims, a Christian interpretive reuse of the Torah's language of near, speakable instruction.

row.basis: heard teaching entrusted for further teaching
row.note: The commentary's protected path carries a received message onward instead of leaving it with one recipient. Timothy is to entrust what he heard before witnesses to reliable people who can teach others, giving a four-stage chain of retained and retransmitted instruction.

row.basis: tradition held in oral word and letter
row.note: The commentary repeatedly holds oral recitation beside pages and written preservation. Paul tells the Thessalonians to stand firm and hold the traditions taught either by spoken word or letter, a compact Christian pairing of memorized and written transmission.

row.basis: the doer rather than the forgetful hearer
row.note: The commentary defines forgetting as leaving an entrusted word and contrasts a merely vocal reading with a life of worship and understanding. James contrasts a forgetful hearer with one who continues in the perfect law and acts on it, making retention visible in conduct.

row.basis: God remembers sin no more as covenantal action
row.note: The commentary stresses that forgetting can mean abandoning rather than a simple failure of mental recall. Jeremiah's promise that God will no longer remember sin uses memory as a covenantal act of judgment or forgiveness, helping a reader hear the commentary's stronger relational sense of forgetting.

row.basis: forgetting even one word of Torah study
row.note: The commentary says 87:6 is assurance rather than a command imposed on the recipient. Avot treats forgetting a word of one's study as grave while qualifying unavoidable loss, placing rabbinic discipline of Torah memory beside the Qur'anic promise that the messenger will not forget.

row.basis: “write this song” read as preserving Torah in writing
row.note: The commentary ends by bringing retained recitation beside earlier pages associated with Moses. Sifre reads Deuteronomy's command to write the song as an injunction to write the Torah, a rabbinic expansion of oral teaching into durable manuscript practice.

row.basis: the enduring book of commandments held fast
row.note: The commentary contrasts gathered, retained revelation with a word discarded as debris. Baruch calls Torah the book of God's commandments that endures forever and sets holding it fast over against death, a Jewish formulation of preservation as life-giving fidelity.

row.basis: the Law burned and people left without its light
row.note: The commentary considers both God's power over revealed speech and the danger of a word being lost. Ezra's lament that the Law has been burned makes the loss of written revelation a concrete crisis rather than merely a lapse of personal memory.

row.basis: Ezra asks for the Spirit so he can write what was lost
row.note: The commentary makes the giver responsible for collecting and securing revelation. In response to the loss of the Law, Ezra asks for the Holy Spirit so that he can write what is needed for later people; the scene is a Jewish restoration analogue to divinely sustained transmission.

row.basis: instruction neither too difficult nor too distant
row.note: The augment links the promise to recite with God's making the way easy. Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or beyond reach, a Torah-side claim that accessible instruction can actually be received and enacted.

row.basis: an easy yoke and light burden
row.note: The commentary places the promised unforgotten word beside the later assurance of ease, while also noting a “weighty word.” Jesus' easy yoke and light burden provide a Christian image for divine teaching that does not finally crush the recipient.

row.basis: mortal life compared to grass and a fading flower
row.note: The commentary has the pasture become dark chaff immediately before the promise of retained recitation. Peter's verse compares all flesh and glory to grass and a flower that withers, supplying the perishable side of the contrast developed explicitly in the next verse.

row.basis: the passing cosmos and imperishable words
row.note: The commentary sets a word that will not be dropped against perishing vegetation. Jesus contrasts heaven and earth passing away with his words not passing away, a Christian saying of verbal permanence that sharpens the commentary's preservation claim.

row.basis: Mary's conception and birth announced by divine speech
row.note: The commentary's secondary image follows Mary as she carries a child and withdraws to give birth. Luke's annunciation likewise joins divine speech to Mary's conception and bearing of a son; the shared Marian scene gives a canonical Christian setting for the commentary's pregnancy image.

row.basis: Mary keeps and ponders words in her heart
row.note: The commentary lets Mary's bodily carrying illuminate a word held within rather than lost. Luke depicts Mary retaining and pondering the reported words in her heart, a Christian maternal image of memory that complements the commentary's contrast between carrying and being forgotten.

row.basis: Adam's transgression narrated as seeing, taking, eating, and giving
row.note: The commentary invokes the Qur'anic Adam who “forgot” an entrusted command as the negative foil to 87:6. Genesis narrates the corresponding fall through the woman's seeing, taking, eating, and giving the fruit, rather than naming Adam's act forgetfulness; the difference changes how disobedience is framed.

row.basis: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws without pages
row.note: The commentary's final page-image attributes earlier sheets to Abraham and Moses. Genesis retrospectively credits Abraham with obeying divine commands and laws but mentions no Abrahamic scroll; that absence is a cautious textual contrast to the Qur'anic “pages of Abraham.”

row.basis: no prophetic word allowed to fall to the ground
row.note: The commentary makes “you will not forget” the result of God-held recitation and contrasts it with a word dropped like worthless debris. Samuel grows with YHWH, who lets none of his words fall to the ground; this prophetic formula gives a close Hebrew Bible image for divinely sustained speech that does not fall away.

row.basis: commandments placed upon the heart
row.note: The commentary has the given word gathered within the recipient before it is voiced. Deuteronomy places these words upon Israel's heart, an early covenant formulation of interior retention that stands behind later oral teaching.

row.basis: words repeatedly taught and spoken in daily life
row.note: The commentary moves from retained recitation to passing the word outwardly. Deuteronomy requires parents to teach the words diligently and speak of them through the ordinary rhythms of day and night, making memory a recurrent oral practice.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's ق ر ء material treats reading as voiced words received by listeners. At the pilgrimage assembly Moses is commanded to read the Torah in all Israel's hearing so that they hear, learn, and fear; the Hebrew קרא is the cognate in a public instructional setting.

row.basis: God's Torah kept in the mouth as a memorial
row.note: The commentary joins unforgotten recitation to memory of the divine giver. Exodus calls the festival sign a memorial so that YHWH's Torah may be in Israel's mouth, making oral retention a ritualized response to deliverance.

row.basis: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
row.note: The commentary brings oral recitation beside the earlier pages of Moses. Before the public reading of the covenant book, Moses writes all YHWH's words; this supplies the written half of the oral-and-page sequence developed in the commentary.

row.basis: testimony bound up and teaching sealed among disciples
row.note: The commentary describes a message whose path to the messenger is guarded and whose retention is secured by its giver. Isaiah orders the testimony bound and the teaching sealed among disciples, a compact image of protected instruction held within a defined receiving community.

row.basis: prophecy inscribed on tablet and book for future time
row.note: The commentary's final pages carry words beyond the first recipient. Isaiah is told to write the message before the people on a tablet and in a book so it remains for a future day, a direct preservation scene for revelation meant to outlast its first utterance.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary pairs gathering with a recited word that is not lost. Isaiah tells hearers to seek and read from YHWH's book, says none will be missing, and grounds the gathering in YHWH's mouth and Spirit; Hebrew קרא supplies the cognate reading verb within an unusually close no-omission context.

row.basis: divine words put in a mouth and protected by God's hand
row.note: The commentary's addressee speaks a word he did not originate and is kept by the speaker who gave it. Isaiah says God has put words in the servant's mouth and covered him with the shadow of the divine hand, joining enabled speech to protection.

row.basis: a word shut up inside that cannot be held back
row.note: The commentary's womb image gives the retained word a later outward release. Jeremiah tries not to mention or speak in God's name, but the word becomes a fire shut in his bones which he cannot contain; it offers a bodily image of inward revelation pressing toward proclamation.

row.basis: God's true word spoken faithfully over against straw
row.note: The commentary puts its undropped word immediately after pasture becomes refuse. Jeremiah distinguishes a dreamer's report from one who has God's word and must speak it faithfully, then contrasts straw with wheat; it joins trustworthy utterance to the commentary's vegetation-and-chaff contrast.

row.basis: God's words found and eaten
row.note: The commentary's language of gathering inside the recipient is not limited to intellectual recall. Jeremiah finds and eats God's words, which become joy and delight, a prophetic ingestion image that complements the scroll-eating scenes without merely repeating them.

row.basis: all divine words received in heart and heard with ears
row.note: The commentary insists that the recipient follows a word first supplied by its teacher. Ezekiel is told to receive in his heart all the words God speaks and to hear them with his ears, explicitly joining inward reception and attentive listening before his mission.

row.basis: God opens the prophet's mouth when speaking to him
row.note: The commentary reads the causative form as God making the addressee able to recite. After controlling Ezekiel's silence, God says that when he speaks with him he will open the prophet's mouth; the verse makes the possibility of prophetic utterance depend on divine initiative.

row.basis: vision written plainly so a reader can run with it
row.note: The commentary holds recitation together with ordered pages and a message carried onward. Habakkuk is told to write the vision clearly on tablets so that its reader may run, a scene where a fixed written revelation enables its bearer to transmit or act on it.

row.basis: Torah read, then confessed and worshipped
row.note: The commentary ends by joining reading to prayer and worship rather than treating it as bare sound. Nehemiah's community spends part of the day reading the Torah and another part confessing and worshipping, a liturgical realization of received words becoming devotion.

row.basis: God-written tablets given to Moses for teaching
row.note: The commentary's “pages of Moses” are words received from God and then given onward. Jubilees has God promise Moses tablets of law and commandment that God has written so Moses may teach them, a Jewish retelling that makes both divine authorship and transmission explicit.

row.basis: the heard word held fast in a good heart and bearing fruit
row.note: The commentary's word is retained in the recipient and subsequently released in beneficial reminder. In Luke's good-soil explanation, hearers hold the word fast in an honest heart and bear fruit with endurance, making fruitful outward consequence depend on inward retention.

row.basis: words received from the Father, given by Jesus, and received by disciples
row.note: The commentary follows revelation from its source through a messenger to those addressed. Jesus says he gave disciples the words the Father gave him and that they received them; this is a three-stage Johannine account of sourced and accepted speech.

row.basis: the Father commands what Jesus must say and speak
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the one who recites from the one who causes the recitation. Jesus says he has not spoken from himself because the Father who sent him commanded what he should say and speak, a closely related claim of divinely determined utterance.

row.basis: the Spirit speaks what it hears and guides into truth
row.note: The commentary has the recipient follow the giver's recitation rather than create an independent message. Jesus describes the Spirit of truth as not speaking from itself but speaking what it hears while guiding disciples, a Christian messenger model of received speech.

row.basis: Spirit-filled believers speak God's word
row.note: The commentary's “we will cause you to recite” attributes enabled proclamation to God. After prayer, the gathered believers are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak God's word with boldness, a communal narrative of divinely empowered speech.

row.basis: words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom
row.note: The commentary frames the recipient's reading as teaching received from a transcendent source. Paul says that he and his colleagues speak in words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom, a Christian articulation of divinely instructed expression.

row.basis: gospel received through revelation rather than human teaching
row.note: The commentary denies that the addressee independently produces the recitation. Paul says he neither received nor was taught his gospel by a human being but received it through revelation of Jesus Christ, a direct source-of-message parallel.

row.basis: God's word received as divine and active within believers
row.note: The commentary says the given word is held within the recipient, not merely heard as an external sound. The Thessalonians receive the preached word as God's word rather than a human one, and Paul says it is at work within believers; this connects reception to inward efficacy.

row.basis: the implanted word received with meekness
row.note: The commentary's pregnancy analogy presents the word as held within a body before outward consequence. James calls the saving word “implanted” and commands its reception, a concise Christian image of a word placed within and able to generate life.

row.basis: new birth through the living and enduring word
row.note: The commentary pairs womb, retention, and release with the word's not being discarded. First Peter attributes new birth to the living and abiding word of God, a Christian use of birth imagery that makes the enduring word generative.

row.basis: Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness
row.note: The commentary's old pages are preserved so their word is not lost. Moses orders the completed Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness; this is a material practice of keeping a received text available beyond immediate oral memory.

row.basis: a sealed book offered to one who says he cannot read it
row.note: The commentary's promise is that God will enable the addressee to recite and will preserve the word, while it also reflects on hidden and manifest speech. Isaiah's vision becomes a sealed book that even a reader cannot read; the contrast makes divine enablement, rather than literacy alone, the issue.

row.basis: instruction written on the tablet of the heart
row.note: The commentary joins pages to a word held in the recipient. Proverbs tells the pupil to bind the commands and write them on the tablet of the heart, a wisdom-text counterpart to inward inscription and memorized guidance.

row.basis: not forgetting God's works while keeping commandments
row.note: The commentary uses forgetting as leaving what has been entrusted and links memory to a later reminder. The psalm's educational purpose is that later generations not forget God's works but keep the commandments, an explicit memory-obedience relation.

row.basis: a book of remembrance for those who fear God and esteem the name
row.note: The commentary connects unforgetting, divine knowledge, and a lasting written record. Malachi describes God attending to those who speak together in reverence and a book of remembrance being written before him, a reciprocal scene of human remembrance and divine record.

row.basis: Moses receives Torah and transmits it through successive teachers
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that a sourced word reaches a recipient and then others. Avot begins its chain with Moses receiving Torah at Sinai and handing it to Joshua, elders, prophets, and the assembly, a rabbinic model of guarded transmission across generations.

row.basis: repeated teaching from Moses through Israel
row.note: The commentary describes the instructor reading first and the recipient following so the word remains. The Talmud's account of Moses teaching Aaron, his sons, elders, and all Israel in repeated cycles makes repetition the concrete practice by which revelation is retained and shared.

row.basis: twenty-four restored books made public for reading
row.note: The commentary sets preserved recitation beside enduring pages and asks how a word reaches later hearers. After Ezra's inspired restoration of books, the Most High orders the first twenty-four made public for worthy and unworthy readers, a Jewish account of recovered revelation opened for communal use.

row.basis: seventy restored books reserved for the wise
row.note: The commentary distinguishes what is openly uttered from what remains hidden under God's control. The next instruction reserves the remaining books for the wise, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpoint in which preservation does not imply unrestricted disclosure.

row.basis: Jewish refusal to add, remove, or alter sacred books
row.note: The commentary claims that the divine source protects the given word from loss and change. Josephus describes a Jewish conviction that no one has dared add to, take from, or alter the ancestral books, a later Jewish articulation of scriptural preservation.

row.basis: apostolic preaching handed on in written Gospels
row.note: The commentary moves from a word received by a messenger to a durable body of pages for later readers. Irenaeus describes the apostles first preaching and then handing down the Gospel in writings, a patristic account of oral revelation becoming preserved Scripture.

row.basis: Spirit gives utterance to the gathered speakers
row.note: The commentary's causative verb makes speech possible through God's action. At Pentecost the gathered disciples begin speaking as the Spirit gives them utterance; the speech is multilingual rather than a recited book, so the link is an enabled-utterance motif.

row.basis: faith comes through hearing the proclaimed word
row.note: The commentary presents recitation as a word carried from its source into the hearer's life. Paul grounds faith in hearing, and hearing in Christ's word, offering a Christian account of oral proclamation as the means by which a message reaches and changes its audience.

row.basis: public reading, exhortation, and teaching
row.note: The commentary treats reading as more than isolated sound: retained words become reminder and instruction. Timothy is charged with public reading, exhortation, and teaching, a church practice that joins recitation to its communal effect.

row.basis: holding fast the taught word in order to exhort others
row.note: The commentary says the recipient must retain the word so that others may be reminded. Titus' overseer holds firmly to the trustworthy word according to teaching in order to exhort and answer opponents, an office-specific parallel to retention becoming instruction.

row.basis: close attention to what was heard lest it drift away
row.note: The commentary's promise removes the danger that the given word will be dropped or forgotten. Hebrews warns hearers to pay closer attention to what they have heard so that they do not drift away, the ordinary human vulnerability against which the Qur'anic assurance stands out.

row.basis: what was heard from the beginning remaining within
row.note: The commentary's gathered word remains in the recipient rather than becoming discarded residue. First John tells believers to let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, making continuance in the received message the condition of continuing communion.
